title: Advanced Military Cryptography
description:
A U.S. Army instructional text on cipher and code systems by the cryptologist William F. Friedman, reprinted by Aegean Park Press from Signal Corps training material. It picks up where an introductory volume leaves off, treating transposition and substitution systems at a more advanced level, with particular attention to systems that combine the two.

The text also covers cryptographs and their limitations, and code systems with an emphasis on enciphered codes. A separate section covers cipher machines: their function, the main types in use, and their relative advantages and disadvantages. The material began as Special Text No. 166 in the Army's extension-course curriculum. The Signal Corps revised it across several editions from the 1930s into the 1940s, and Aegean Park Press then issued this civilian reprint.

Friedman wrote it during his long tenure directing the Army's cryptologic training and research. He came to cryptology as a geneticist at George Fabyan's Riverbank Laboratories in Illinois. There he and his wife Elizebeth Smith Friedman turned a private research post into wartime code-breaking work. He founded and led the Army's Signal Intelligence Service starting in 1929, and later directed the team that broke the Japanese PURPLE cipher and helped design the SIGABA cipher machine.

The series numbering is inconsistently reported across dealers and could not be independently confirmed. Page count also varies by listing (113 vs. 116pp). Some copies of this same ISBN carry a 1996 date on the title/copyright page rather than 1976; both appear to be printings of the same Aegean Park Press edition rather than distinct revisions.

title: Manual for the Solution of Military Ciphers
description:
The first cipher manual issued by the U.S. Army, written by Captain Parker Hitt and originally printed by the Press of the Army Service Schools at Fort Leavenworth in 1916. This Aegean Park Press edition, part of its Cryptographic Series, reprints Hitt's plain, example-driven approach to solving unknown ciphers.

The text opens with Hitt's well-known statement of what solving a cipher demands: perseverance, careful method, intuition, and luck. From there it works through monoalphabetic and polyalphabetic substitution and simple transposition systems, using real intercepted cryptograms of the period. Solutions are explained step by step, with further problems left for the reader to work through.

Hitt was an Army Signal Corps officer and instructor at the Signal School at Fort Leavenworth when he wrote the manual, drawing on his own success solving Mexican revolutionary-era ciphers. His cylindrical cipher device, developed around the same period, was later adapted by Joseph Mauborgne into the M-94 strip cipher issued to the Army and Navy. His sliding-strip variant became the basis for the M-138-A. He served in France with the American Expeditionary Forces during World War I, running AEF coding and decoding, and retired a colonel. He is widely credited as the founder of systematic American military cryptology.
tags: Cryptography, Cryptanalysis, Codes and Ciphers, Military History, World War I

This record describes the 1976 Aegean Park Press reprint; a distinct 1918 second edition of the original also exists (per the cryptobooks.org bibliography, bookid 478) but its bibliographic details could not be confirmed and it is not the edition catalogued here.

title: Cryptography and Cryptanalysis Articles, Volume 1
contributors: Marcel Givierge (Contributor); Alf Monge (Contributor); Howell C. Brown (Contributor)
description:
A collection of previously classified cryptology articles from the Army's Signal Corps Bulletin. William F. Friedman gathered and edited them; Aegean Park Press reprinted the set as Volume 1 of two, meant as collateral reading for students of cryptography and cryptanalysis.

This volume contains four articles: Friedman's own "Cryptanalysis," Marcel Givierge's "Problems of Code," Alf Monge's "Solution of the Playfair Cipher," and Howell C. Brown's "Analysis Versus the Probable Word." It closes with an appendix of Playfair cipher problems added for the student. It appeared in 1976 as No. 5 in Aegean Park Press's Cryptographic Series; a companion Volume 2 followed as No. 6.

Friedman edited and largely wrote the material collected here during his years directing Army cryptologic training between the world wars. He had come to cryptology as a geneticist at George Fabyan's Riverbank Laboratories, where he and his wife Elizebeth Smith Friedman did wartime code-breaking work. He then joined the Army's Signal Intelligence Service, which he founded and led starting in 1929. His Signal Corps training texts, including these Bulletin articles, shaped how a generation of American cryptanalysts learned the field before Friedman went on to direct the breaking of the Japanese PURPLE cipher.

title: Cryptography and Cryptanalysis Articles, Volume 2
description:
The companion volume to Aegean Park Press's Cryptography and Cryptanalysis Articles, Volume 1: a second gathering of previously classified cryptology articles originally printed in the Army's Signal Corps Bulletin, edited by William F. Friedman and issued in 1976 as No. 6 in the publisher's Cryptographic Series (Volume 1 was No. 5).

Bookseller listings for this volume were found to be inconsistent, several apparently reusing Volume 1's article list and description rather than describing this book's actual contents. No source consulted could be confirmed as describing Volume 2's specific articles independently of that overlap, so this record does not assert which pieces it contains. What can be said with more confidence is the shared premise of the series: the publisher's stated purpose was to collect Signal Corps Bulletin articles on cryptography and cryptanalysis, most previously classified, into single volumes as collateral reading for students of the field.

title: The Riverbank Publications, Volume 1
edition_printrun: Aegean Park Press facsimile reprint (Cryptographic Series, C-23)
description:
The Riverbank Publications, Volume 1 gathers the first four of William F. Friedman's foundational monographs on cipher-solving, reprinted in facsimile by Aegean Park Press from pamphlets George Fabyan's Riverbank Laboratories issued between 1917 and 1922.

This volume contains Publication No. 15, A Method of Reconstructing the Primary Alphabet From a Single One of the Series of Secondary Alphabets; No. 16, Methods for the Solution of Running-Key Ciphers; No. 17, An Introduction to Methods for the Solution of Ciphers; and No. 18, Synoptic Tables for the Solution of Ciphers and a Bibliography of Cipher Literature. These were written at Riverbank's Department of Ciphers in Geneva, Illinois. The original printings were short, restricted at the time as wartime material. Friedman used them as his own textbooks when he trained American servicemen in cryptanalysis in 1917. Aegean Park Press later reissued the series as a three-volume set. This volume covers No. 15-18. A second volume reprints No. 19-21. A third reprints No. 22, The Index of Coincidence and Its Applications in Cryptography.

Friedman directed Riverbank's cipher department before moving to the War Department. There he became the US Army's chief cryptologist. He is generally regarded as the central figure in the emergence of American cryptology as a formal discipline. Elizebeth Smith Friedman, his wife and Riverbank colleague, contributed to the department's work over the same years.

title: Solving German Codes in World War I
description:
Solving German Codes in World War I is William F. Friedman's technical account of how German code systems, as distinct from cipher systems, were broken during the First World War, reissued by Aegean Park Press with, per its cover, "an added special code problem for the student."

The text covers how intercepted messages were prepared for study, the main classes of German code groups and their characteristics, solution by analogy to previously solved material, and the enciphering tables the Germans layered on top of their codebooks to complicate solution. Friedman appends a practice code problem in English so the reader can apply the methods he describes. The German trench codebook Satzbuch 140, reproduced on the cover, is representative of the field codes the text addresses.

Friedman worked on German codebooks as part of the American Expeditionary Forces' intelligence effort in France, building on the cryptanalytic training he had developed at Riverbank Laboratories before the war. He went on to become the US Army's chief cryptologist and one of the principal architects of American cryptology as a discipline.
tags: Cryptography, Cryptanalysis, Codes and Ciphers, World War I, Military History
notes: Aegean Park Press Cryptographic Series (Laguna Hills, CA). A second Aegean Park edition exists under ISBN 0894120190; this record uses ISBN 9780894121180, the edition documented on Amazon and AbeBooks. title: The History of Codes and Ciphers in the United States Prior to World War I
description:
The History of Codes and Ciphers in the United States Prior to World War I, edited by Wayne G. Barker, opens Aegean Park Press's multi-volume history of American cryptology, tracing the subject from its early roots up to the outbreak of the First World War.

According to the Smithsonian Institution Libraries' catalog record, the book corresponds to Volume 1 of "Historical Background of the Signal Security Agency." The Army Security Agency's Historical Section wrote that study in 1946; it was later declassified. Barker's companion volume, The History of Codes and Ciphers in the United States During World War I, continues it as Volume 2. A further volume in the series covers the interwar years, 1919-1929. This volume itself runs 159 pages, with facsimiles and illustrations of period cryptographic material.

Barker founded Aegean Park Press in 1973. He edited a substantial share of its Cryptographic Series, drawing on declassified US government material to document the history of American code-breaking through the Army Security Agency's own internal records.

Wayne Barker founded Aegean Park Press in 1973 and edited much of its Cryptographic Series, including this history and its companion volumes on World War I and the interwar years.

title: Treatise on Cryptography
edition_printrun: Aegean Park Press, Cryptographic Series (English translation)
description:
Treatise on Cryptography is Aegean Park Press's English edition of André Lange and E.-A. Soudart's Traité de Cryptographie, first published in Paris by Librairie Félix Alcan in 1925.

The original French text opens with five chapters tracing the history of cryptography from antiquity to the early twentieth century. It then turns to technical treatment of transposition methods, substitution methods, codes, cryptographic devices, and cipher machines, illustrated with roughly 100 tables and drawings across 366 pages. The Aegean Park edition presents this material in English, not in facsimile French. A Google Books record for the English edition credits the US Office of the Chief of Naval Operations as a contributor. That points to Aegean Park having reprinted an existing US Navy translation of the work, rather than commissioning a new one.

Lange and Soudart's treatise is counted among the standard general studies of cryptography from the interwar period. It sits alongside works such as Givierge's Cours de Cryptographie and Figl's Systeme des Chiffrierens. Together, these shaped cryptology before the rise of machine cryptanalysis.

Pierrepont, assisted by H.H. Handley" -- consistent with Aegean Park having reprinted that 1940 US Navy translation, though this record could not confirm the translator credit appears on the Aegean Park printing itself. title: The Contribution of the Cryptographic Bureaus in the World War
description:
Yves Gyldén's survey compares the codebreaking organizations of the Allied and Central Powers in the First World War. It was one of the first attempts by a working cryptologist to weigh what each side's cryptographic bureau achieved and where it fell short.

The book was first published in Swedish, in Stockholm in 1931, as Chifferbyråernas insatser i världskriget till lands. An English translation ran in the U.S. Army Signal Corps Bulletin, nos. 75-81, from November 1933 to November 1934. Aegean Park Press then issued it as a standalone volume in its Cryptographic Series. William F. Friedman edited the translation from Swedish and added his own comments to the text.

Gyldén came to cryptology through family connections to the Swedish cipher industry. His father Olof Gyldén helped found the Cryptograph company with engineer Arvid Damm, the firm that later produced the machines associated with Boris Hagelin. Yves Gyldén taught cryptology and cryptanalysis at Swedish military schools and was regarded, through the 1930s, as Sweden's leading authority on the subject.

title: Solution of the Voynich Manuscript: A Liturgical Manual for the Endura Rite of the Cathari Heresy, the Cult of Isis
description:
Leo Levitov's 1987 book makes a specific claim about the Voynich manuscript, the medieval codex that has resisted every attempted decipherment since its rediscovery in 1912. He argues it is a liturgical manual for the Endura, the Cathar deathbed rite, written in a Flemish-based dialect, and that Catharism itself was a continuation of the ancient cult of Isis.

Levitov lays out his method in the book. He identifies a recurring pattern-word he reads as ISIS and builds a phonetic transliteration of the manuscript's script from it, then offers translated passages to support the liturgical reading. He treats the manuscript's resistance to decipherment as consistent with the Inquisition's near-total destruction of Cathar literature, which he argues left few records to check his reading against.

Voynich manuscript specialists have not accepted this decipherment. Linguist Jacques Guy and researcher Dennis Stallings published detailed critiques in the years after publication, citing the manuscript's later radiocarbon dating, which places it after Catharism's suppression, and the absence of a clear French or Occitan textual signature. The claim is catalogued here as Levitov's argument, not as an established reading of the manuscript.
tags: Voynich Manuscript, Cryptanalysis, Codes and Ciphers, Cryptography
notes: Levitov's decipherment is not accepted by Voynich manuscript scholarship. Detailed critiques were published by linguist Jacques Guy ("On Levitov's Decipherment of the Voynich Manuscript," 1991) and researcher Dennis J. Stallings (1998).

author_full_name: J.W. Bennett, W.A. Hobart, J.B. Spitzer
title: Intelligence and Cryptanalytic Activities of the Japanese During World War II, Volume 1
description:
This is the published edition of a 1945 U.S. Army intelligence study. It was declassified decades later and issued commercially as the first of a multi-volume Aegean Park Press set. The set documents how Japan's intelligence services were organized and how well, or badly, they read Allied communications during the Second World War.

The report was compiled by the Military Intelligence Service of the War Department General Staff, known as MIS/WDGS. It was later declassified by the National Security Agency under its Special Research History series, as SRH-254. This first volume, subtitled The Japanese Intelligence System, MIS/WDGS, covers the organization and operating methods of Japan's wartime intelligence apparatus. A companion volume in the set addresses Japanese cryptanalytic activity specifically.

Aegean Park Press, a Laguna Hills, California publisher that specialized in reprinting declassified cryptologic and intelligence material, issued the volume in 1986. Authorship is credited to J.W. Bennett, W.A. Hobart, and J.B. Spitzer, the U.S. Army officers who compiled the original 1945 study.

title: The Enigma Symposium 1994
description:
Hugh Skillen's self-published record documents the second annual Enigma Reunion, a gathering of Bletchley Park and Y Service veterans held in Bedford in 1994. It collects their personal accounts of Britain's wartime signals intelligence work alongside Skillen's own commentary and documentation.

Skillen edited and issued a volume from each of these reunions through the 1990s and into the early 2000s. This one runs to roughly 119 pages: six of front matter plus 113 pages of text, with 26 pages of illustrations, diagrams, and photographs. Few libraries hold it, and this record is built largely from booksellers' physical descriptions rather than a library catalogue entry.

Skillen was himself a Y Service veteran and a trained linguist who worked in wartime signals intelligence. After the war he returned to teaching French at Harrow County School for Boys. In later life he devoted himself to recording the wartime work of his Bletchley Park and Y Service colleagues. He self-published this symposium series from his home in Pinner, Middlesex, alongside book-length histories including Spies of the Airwaves.

title: The Enigma Symposium 1995
description:
The Enigma Symposium 1995 is the self-published proceedings of the third Enigma Reunion, convened and printed by Hugh Skillen in a small run at Pinner, Middlesex.

The 164-page volume, issued with illustrated green card covers and an eight-page preliminary section, collects the personal wartime accounts of Bletchley Park and Y Service veterans who worked in Allied signals intelligence during the Second World War. As with Skillen's other symposium volumes, the material is firsthand testimony gathered from reunion attendees rather than formal scholarship.

Skillen served in the Intelligence Corps during the war and later wrote a self-published trilogy on the Army's Y Service (Spies of the Airwaves, 1989; Knowledge Strengthens the Arm, 1990; Enigma and Its Achilles Heel, 1992) before organizing the annual Enigma Reunions and publishing their proceedings himself through the 1990s.

title: The Enigma Symposium 1999
description:
The Enigma Symposium 1999 is Hugh Skillen's self-published record of the sixth Enigma Reunion, issued as an oversized softcover with glossy green covers.

Running to 210 pages, it continues the format of Skillen's earlier symposium volumes: firsthand wartime testimony from veterans of Bletchley Park and the Y Service's signals intelligence work, illustrated throughout with black-and-white photographs. A color photograph near the front of the book shows the author and fellow veterans at the Imperial War Museum in 1997.

Skillen, a former Intelligence Corps officer, wrote the trilogy Spies of the Airwaves (1989), Knowledge Strengthens the Arm (1990), and Enigma and Its Achilles Heel (1992) documenting the Army's Y Service before turning to the Enigma Reunions, which he convened and published proceedings for annually through the 1990s.

title: Masked Dispatches: Cryptograms and Cryptology in American History, 1775-1900
publisher: Center for Cryptologic History, National Security Agency
description:
Masked Dispatches: Cryptograms and Cryptology in American History, 1775-1900 is a National Security Agency history of American cryptology before the twentieth century, written by Ralph E. Weber with a foreword by David W. Gaddy. It is Volume 1 of the NSA Center for Cryptologic History's United States Cryptologic History, Series I: Pre-World War I, first published in 1993 and later reissued, including a third edition in 2013.

The 227-page volume traces American cryptography from the Continental Congress's United Colonies' Cipher through the coded diplomatic and Civil War-era correspondence of the nineteenth century, drawing on the papers of figures including James Lovell and State Department codebook author John Haswell. It covers the period before wireless communication, when codes and ciphers moved by messenger and handwritten correspondence rather than electronic transmission.

Weber was professor emeritus of history at Marquette University and worked on deciphering coded material in the papers of Presidents John Adams and Woodrow Wilson. Gaddy, who contributed the foreword, was a charter member of the Senior Cryptologic Executive Service. The book is distributed free by the NSA's Center for Cryptologic History and is available as a PDF from the agency.

notes: United States Cryptologic History, Series I: Pre-World War I, Volume 1. First published 1993; reissued in later printings including a third edition in 2013. title: A Priceless Advantage: U.S. Navy Communications Intelligence and the Battles of Coral Sea, Midway, and the Aleutians
publisher: Center for Cryptologic History, National Security Agency
description:
A Priceless Advantage: U.S. Navy Communications Intelligence and the Battles of Coral Sea, Midway, and the Aleutians documents how Navy codebreaking shaped three Pacific campaigns of 1942. Frederick D. Parker wrote it for the NSA's Center for Cryptologic History. It is Volume 5 of the agency's United States Cryptologic History, Series IV: World War II. The NSA first published it in 1993, revised it in a second edition in 2011, and reissued it in 2017 for the seventy-fifth anniversary of Midway.

Parker draws on surviving COMINT records held by NSA, the military services, and the National Archives. He shows how communications intelligence helped Admiral Chester W. Nimitz, Commander in Chief of the Pacific Fleet. The report calls it a "priceless advantage" in the battles of Coral Sea and Midway. Parker also covers the Aleutians campaign, an episode he notes other historians have often left out, and describes one instance where COMINT was available to a task force commander but went unused.

Parker served in the U.S. Marine Corps in 1943-45 and 1950-52. He held a B.S. from Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service. He retired from NSA in 1984 after thirty-two years of service. Afterward he continued the work as a volunteer and reemployed annuitant at the Center for Cryptologic History, where he also wrote on Navy communications intelligence in the Pearl Harbor period.

title: The National Cryptologic Museum Activities Book: Codes, Ciphers, and Puzzles
description:
A 22-page activity booklet produced in 1996 by the NSA's Center for Cryptologic History, issued in connection with the National Cryptologic Museum at Fort George G. Meade, Maryland.

The booklet presents a set of cipher and puzzle exercises for museum visitors, covering basic substitution and transposition techniques rather than offering a history or reference text. No individual author or compiler is credited; it was produced as an institutional publication of the Center for Cryptologic History, the NSA office that also oversees the museum's historical and library holdings.

notes: Corporate publication of the NSA Center for Cryptologic History; no ISBN or individual author found in library or bookseller records checked.

title: United States Cryptographic Patents, 1861-1989
description:
United States Cryptographic Patents, 1861-1989 is a 115-page reference work compiled by Jack Levine. It lists every U.S. patent granted for cryptographic devices and methods across more than a century, from an 1861 telegraph-register patent through patents issued in the late 1980s.

The patents are arranged in two separate sequences: one in chronological order by patent date, and a second alphabetical by inventor. The volume works either as a timeline of cryptographic invention or as a lookup tool for a specific patent holder. A number of entries are illustrated with drawings of the cipher machines and devices described in the patents. This is a second, expanded edition, superseding a shorter 1983 printing that covered patents only through 1981.

Levine was a mathematician at North Carolina State University whose research spanned differential geometry, combinatorics, and tensor analysis. He also had a sustained interest in cryptology, publishing a four-volume study of pattern word lists used in cryptanalysis and contributing regularly to Cryptologia, the journal that issued this volume. His papers, including his cryptographic patent research, are held by the NC State University Libraries.
tags: Cryptography, Reference, Patents
notes: Second, expanded edition of Levine's cryptographic patent bibliography, covering patents through 1989; an earlier 80-page edition covering only 1861-1981 was co-authored with Louis Kruh and published in 1983.

title: Cracking Codes: The Rosetta Stone and Decipherment
contributors: Whitfield Diffie (Contributor); Mary Fischer (Contributor); R. S. Simpson (Contributor)
description:
Published by the British Museum Press in 1999, Cracking Codes accompanied an exhibition at the British Museum marking the two-hundredth anniversary of the Rosetta Stone's discovery. Richard Parkinson, then Assistant Keeper in the museum's Department of Egyptian Antiquities, wrote the book. It traces how the stone's parallel inscriptions in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek were used to unlock the Egyptian scripts.

The 208-page book follows the competing efforts of Thomas Young and Jean-Francois Champollion to read the stone. It then widens out to the social and practical uses of writing in ancient Egypt, the relationship between hieroglyphs and pictorial art, and related decipherment cases including Linear B and Meroitic script. A selective catalogue of the exhibition's objects runs alongside the main text, with contributions from Whitfield Diffie, Mary Fischer, and R. S. Simpson.

Parkinson worked in the British Museum's Department of Ancient Egypt and Sudan for more than two decades. Alongside that curatorial work, he published widely on Middle Kingdom literature and Egyptian poetry.
tags: Codes and Ciphers, Decipherment, Reference

title: The Secret History of KGB Spy Cameras: 1945-1995
description:
The Secret History of KGB Spy Cameras: 1945-1995, published by Schiffer Publishing in 2018, traces the development and field use of Soviet subminiature cameras built for espionage. It was written by intelligence historian H. Keith Melton together with Lt. Col. Vladimir Alekseenko, a career KGB technical intelligence officer who worked in Soviet stations across Europe and the United States. Alekseenko provided operational and technical support, including protection against eavesdropping on Soviet missions, and camera collectors Michael M. Hasco and Detlev Vreisleben contributed additional material.

Across 192 pages and more than 400 photographs, the book covers over ninety camera systems used by the KGB and, to a lesser extent, the GRU. These were used for copying documents, conducting surveillance, and compromising targets. A glossary at the end catalogues KGB and GRU photographic and optical systems and equipment terminology. Alekseenko died of cancer as the book was being completed, so the account draws on the direct testimony of an officer who used this equipment operationally.

Melton is an intelligence historian and a founding board member of the International Spy Museum in Washington, D.C. He has written extensively on clandestine technology and Cold War tradecraft, and the same author team followed this book with a companion volume on Stasi spy cameras.
tags: Espionage, Surveillance, Military History, Cold War

title: Break the Code: Cryptography for Beginners
description:
Break the Code: Cryptography for Beginners is a Dover instructional activity book that teaches six basic cipher techniques through step-by-step examples aimed at young and first-time readers.

The book walks through simple letter grouping, reverse trail, shift code, key word code, date shift code, and twisted path code, each explained in plain terms and followed by practice messages for the reader to encode and decode; 51 practice messages appear across the book, illustrated with cartoons by Larry Daste. A glossary of cryptographic terms, a sheet of reproducible graph paper, and ready-made cipher alphabets round out the material, with solutions printed at the back.

Dover published it in 1997 as a "Dover Original," 71 pages (Z103.J65 1997; OCLC 36817271). Little else about Bud Johnson's career is documented; publisher copy describes him as a former military cryptographer, though that claim could not be independently verified here.
tags: Cryptography, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles, Children's Books
notes: Marketed as a "Dover Original" in period listings and library records; searches for an earlier edition under a different imprint (the hypothesis in the research assignment) turned up no evidence, so it appears to be a first edition from Dover rather than a reissue. title: Identity, Privacy, and Personal Freedom: Big Brother vs. the New Resistance
description:
Identity, Privacy, and Personal Freedom: Big Brother vs. the New Resistance is a 1999 instructional manual from Paladin Press on reducing a person's exposure to government and institutional tracking through everyday identification and record systems.

Sheldon Charrett covers the Social Security card and other identification documents, along with practical steps for handling mail, telephone service, internet access, banking, employment, and marriage records with less traceable identifying information. Library of Congress subject headings for the book include forgeries, identification cards, and right of privacy (LCCN 00268414).

Paladin Press, based in Boulder, Colorado, published manuals on personal freedom, self-reliance, and related practical-skills subjects for a specialist mail-order and retail readership from 1970 until it closed in 2018. Charrett's related title, The Modern Identity Changer (Paladin Press, 1997), covers overlapping ground on constructing a new identity.
tags: Privacy, Surveillance, Reference
notes: A related title by the same author and publisher, The Modern Identity Changer (Paladin Press, 1997, ISBN 9780873649469), covers overlapping subject matter; the two are distinct books, not variant editions of one another. A print-on-demand-looking reprint ISBN (9781984043580, dated September 1999) surfaced in one retailer listing; it was not independently confirmed and is not used here. Subjects (LOC): Forgeries; Identification cards; Right of privacy.

title: Compilation of State and Federal Privacy Laws
edition_printrun: unresolved — a serially updated compilation with many editions confirmed (1976, 1977, 1978, 1981, 1992, 1997, 2000, 2002, 2003, and a 2013 edition with a 2018 supplement); which edition/printing this record describes could not be established
description:
Compilation of State and Federal Privacy Laws is a serially updated legal reference published by Privacy Journal. It gathers federal and state statutes that touch on personal privacy into a single volume.

Editions were issued roughly every few years starting in 1975. The first compilation listed about 50 privacy laws; later editions tracked the subject's growth, reaching roughly 200 laws by 1976, 500 by 1984, 600 by 1988, and over 1,000 by 1997. Editions are organized by subject heading, covering areas such as credit reporting, government records, and workplace and genetic testing, with appendices of representative statutes. Later editions added a supplement rather than a full reprint, including a 2013 edition with a 2018 supplement. This record could not establish which specific edition or printing is being described; the edition field is left unresolved rather than guessed.

Robert Ellis Smith (1940-2018) was a lawyer and journalist. He founded and edited the Privacy Journal newsletter starting in 1974, and the Compilation was one of his signature ongoing publications alongside it. He continued to edit successive editions of the Compilation for more than 40 years.
tags: Privacy, Reference, Law
notes: This is a serial reference work reissued in many editions; no ISBN, year, page count, or edition number is asserted here because the specific copy/edition was not established. If the physical copy on hand has a visible copyright year or edition statement, that should be checked against the shelf book and this record updated before publishing.

title: The Ultimate Cellular Phone Security Manual
description:
A mail-order technical manual on cellular telephone security from Consumertronics, the New Mexico publisher run by John J. Williams that supplied the 1980s and 1990s electronic-countermeasures underground.

No catalogue record for this exact title was found in OpenLibrary, the Library of Congress or WorldCat. Consumertronics documented a closely related Williams title, Cellular & Cordless Guide, covering analog-era cloning and reprogramming, ESN and MIN data, scanning and monitoring, and countermeasures under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act. Whether the manual held here is that book under another name or a separate publication has not been established; the title page of the copy on the shelf would settle it.

Williams ran Consumertronics from New Mexico from the early 1980s into the 2000s, issuing manuals on telephone systems, cellular fraud, computer file security and related electronics. The company sold directly by post and advertised in the hobbyist and survivalist press, outside the trade channels that produce library records, which is why its output is documented so unevenly. Its cellular titles belong to the analog era, before digital and encrypted standards closed off the monitoring these manuals described.
tags: Privacy, Surveillance, Reference
notes: The exact title "The Ultimate Cellular Phone Security Manual" could not be confirmed in OpenLibrary, WorldCat, or the Library of Congress catalog after multiple searches. It may be an alternate or informal title for Consumertronics' documented "Cellular & Cordless Guide" by the same author (ISBN 9780934274555), or a genuine separate title not indexed by these catalogues; this could not be resolved. If the physical copy is in hand, check its title page and copyright page directly and correct this record.

title: The Spy Code Handbook: How to Make Code and Cipher Machines to Outfox Your Enemies
description:
A hands-on activity book that shows children how to build twelve code and cipher devices, the kind spies have used for centuries, using only a pencil, scissors, card and glue.

Each device comes with instructions for making it and for writing and decoding secret messages. Notes cover how to complicate a cipher so it becomes harder to crack, even for another reader of the book. It's a step-by-step project book for kids, not a history or reference text.

Duncan Ball is an Australian children's author best known for the Selby and Emily Eyefinger series. He wrote The Spy Code Handbook with his son Ian Ball; Stephen Case illustrated it. The book appeared under several titles and imprints through the 1990s, including a UK Collins hardcover in the \"Activity Books\" series and an Australian edition marketed as \"Ashtons Spy Code Handbook.\"
tags: Children's Books, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles, Espionage
notes: Multiple editions and titles exist: Collins (UK) hardcover 1991, ISBN 9780001963849, listed under the series "Activity Books"; Angus & Robertson (UK) paperback, ISBN 9780207177187; and an Australian variant issued as "Ashtons Spy Code Handbook," ISBN 9780000194381. All credit Duncan Ball and Ian Ball as authors and Stephen Case as illustrator. This record uses the original 1990 Angus & Robertson (Sydney) paperback edition, ISBN 9780207160189, per a bookseller (Willis Monie) cataloging it as a 1990 second printing; OpenLibrary's record for the same ISBN instead lists "HarperCollins Publishers Canada" and 1992, which looks like a generic/distributor catalog entry rather than the title-page imprint, so it is not used here.

title: Codes & Ciphers
description:
A puzzle-book built entirely around coded messages: readers follow a story of five adventurers and must decipher each code in turn to keep the plot moving, working through substitution, transposition and other basic cipher types along the way.

It was published as the \"Advanced Level\" volume in Usborne's Superpuzzles series, sitting alongside the series' map, maze and logic-puzzle titles; a solutions section at the back lets readers check their answers. Later printings were distributed in North America through EDC Publishing, Usborne's US partner.
tags: Children's Books, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles, Cryptography
notes: Part of the Usborne Superpuzzles series, designated "Advanced Level" on the cover (a series/level marker, not a subtitle). AbeBooks and OpenLibrary both list the publisher of the 1995 paperback printing (ISBN 9780746006757) as "EDC Publishing," the North American distributor for Usborne; Goodreads attributes the same printing to Usborne Publishing Ltd, and the ISBN itself carries Usborne's own 0746 prefix, so this record follows Usborne as publisher of record. A separate library-binding edition, ISBN 9780881105261, was issued in the US by EDC Publishing under its own prefix.

title: Lu & Clancy's Secret Codes
description:
An activity-mystery book built around sixteen codes readers must decipher to help two dog detectives, Lu and a basset hound named Clancy, track down Lu's missing sister.

The codes range from familiar backwards writing and number substitution to less common forms: a musical code, a pinprick code, a crossword-style code, and one based on the ancient ogham alphabet, illustrated using broken pieces of spaghetti. Each code comes with a practice message, and the answer key at the back is paired with a set of forensic-science puzzles.

The book is part of Mason's longer-running Lu & Clancy series for Kids Can Press, which continued with titles including The Carnival Caper and Sound Off, pairing mystery-solving with hands-on science and puzzle activities for young readers.
tags: Children's Books, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles, Cryptography
notes: First title in Adrienne Mason's Lu & Clancy activity-mystery series for Kids Can Press; later series entries include The Carnival Caper (2002) and Sound Off (2002).

title: The Nancy Drew Secret-Code Activity Book
description:
A puzzle-and-activity book licensed to the Nancy Drew franchise, built around secret-code and cipher puzzles for young readers to solve.

Unlike the Nancy Drew mystery novels themselves, which appear under the house pseudonym Carolyn Keene, this activity book is credited on its title page to Nancy T. Rockwell for the text and Tony Tallarico for the illustrations. Tallarico, a longtime comic-book artist, illustrated several other Nancy Drew tie-in activity books for Grosset & Dunlap in the same period, including the numbered Nancy Drew Mystery Activity Book series.
tags: Children's Books, Codes and Ciphers, Puzzles
notes: No Carolyn Keene byline appears on this title; it is credited to Nancy T. Rockwell (text) and Tony Tallarico (illustrations). Some bookseller listings credit Tallarico first or list him alone, but a detailed listing (Biblio) explicitly labels him "(Illustrator)" against Rockwell's unlabeled (text/author) credit, which this record follows.

title: Codes and Ciphers
publisher: Compass Books / Geoffrey Cumberlege, Oxford University Press
edition_printrun: Compass Books edition, "revised and reset" (1949 printing)
description:
Codes and Ciphers is a general-audience survey of cryptography. Alexander D'Agapeyeff, a Russian-born London cartographer with no formal training in the field, wrote it on commission for Oxford University Press as war approached in 1939. It moves through the history of secret writing from classical substitution ciphers to the code and cipher systems then in commercial and military use.

On the book's final page D'Agapeyeff set a 400-digit challenge cryptogram inviting readers to test their skill against it. No one has solved it. D'Agapeyeff later said he could no longer remember how he had encrypted the passage. By his son's account he was embarrassed by the episode, and cryptographers have continued to attempt the cipher into the twenty-first century. Accounts differ on when the puzzle was dropped from the book. The standard secondhand-trade description states it appeared only in the 1939 first edition; a collector who compared physical copies found it still present in the 1949 Compass Books printing and removed only from 1952 onward. This copy is the 1949 Compass Books edition (Compass Books / Geoffrey Cumberlege, Oxford University Press), revised and reset to 149 pages. Its exact printing has not been confirmed against a physical inspection of the copyright page, so whether this specific copy carries the cipher is not established.

D'Agapeyeff had written an earlier manual on cartography for the same press and took on this book as a commercial assignment rather than as a specialist in the subject. Codes and Ciphers went through several editions between 1939 and the 1970s. It is remembered today chiefly for the challenge cipher that its own author forgot how to solve.
tags: Codes and Ciphers, Cryptography, Puzzles
notes: Bibliographic uncertainty, disclosed rather than resolved: this copy is identified as the Compass Books / Geoffrey Cumberlege, Oxford University Press printing dated 1949 on an AbeBooks dealer listing for that exact edition (revised and reset, 149pp). Sources conflict on when the famous D'Agapeyeff challenge cipher was dropped from the book: the common secondhand-trade claim is 'first edition only' (1939); a collector who directly compared physical copies (Cipher Mysteries blog) reports the cipher still present in a 1949 copy and absent from 1952 onward. A physical inspection of this exact copy's copyright/impression statement was not possible, so its cipher status is reported here as unconfirmed rather than asserted either way. This 1949 printing predates the ISBN system, so it has no ISBN. A reliable period cover image for the 1949 Compass Books printing could not be sourced within the research budget, so cover_image is left null pending a photograph of the physical copy.

title: Capturing Enigma: How HMS Petard Seized the German Naval Codes
edition_printrun: First edition (a paperback reissue followed from The History Press, ISBN 9780750930505)
description:
Capturing Enigma reconstructs the October 1942 boarding of the sinking German submarine U-559 in the eastern Mediterranean. It was this action that recovered the Enigma cipher material Bletchley Park needed to break the German navy's upgraded four-rotor U-boat code.

Harper follows the British destroyer HMS Petard through its wartime service. He focuses on the night two of its crew, Colin Grazier and Tommy Brown, swam to the abandoned U-559 and passed code books and cipher settings up through the conning tower before the submarine sank under them. The intelligence recovered ended a ten-month blackout in Allied U-boat tracking and is credited with turning the Battle of the Atlantic. Grazier and Brown's actions were kept secret at the time under the wartime restrictions on Ultra intelligence, and the two men were rewarded only with the George Cross rather than the Victoria Cross that had been proposed. The book also covers Petard's broader Mediterranean service beyond the single action named in its title.

Harper served as a coder aboard HMS Petard during the ship's second wartime commission and later worked for two decades as a Daily Express foreign correspondent. Capturing Enigma draws on his own service history and on interviews with surviving crew, and sits alongside his other wartime narrative histories, Miracle of Deliverance and Last Sunset.
tags: Enigma, World War II, Signals Intelligence, Military History
notes: Reader reviews (Goodreads) note the book covers HMS Petard's broader wartime service in more detail than the single Enigma-capture episode named in the title; reflected in the description above rather than overstated.

title: Fermat's Enigma: The Epic Quest to Solve the World's Greatest Mathematical Problem
edition_printrun: First US edition (published in the UK the same year as Fermat's Last Theorem)
description:
Fermat's Enigma tells the story of Fermat's Last Theorem. Pierre de Fermat left it unproved in a 1637 margin note, claiming a proof too large to fit the page. The search for that proof lasted 358 years before Andrew Wiles closed it in 1994.

Singh traces the theorem through the mathematicians who attempted and failed to prove it, including Euler, Sophie Germain, Cauchy, Lame, and Kummer. He then turns to Wiles, who worked in secrecy for seven years at Princeton. Wiles's approach connected the problem to the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture linking elliptic curves and modular forms, a link Ken Ribet had shown would settle Fermat's theorem if proved. Wiles's first announced proof, in 1993, contained a gap that took another year of work with Richard Taylor to close. This US edition carries a foreword by John Lynch, who directed the BBC documentary The Proof on which the book is based. The UK edition was published as Fermat's Last Theorem.

Singh is a BBC science journalist with a doctorate in particle physics from Cambridge. This was his first book. It became the first mathematics book to reach number one on the UK bestseller list, and he went on to write The Code Book, a history of cryptography, and Big Bang.
tags: Cryptography, Puzzles
notes: Fermat's Last Theorem itself is number theory, not cryptography; catalogued in the cryptology wing at the user's direction as a companion title to the wing's cryptography/mathematics holdings. Tags reflect that: 'Puzzles' and 'Cryptography' fit loosely (Singh's later career and the book's puzzle-solving narrative arc), no closer match exists in the fixed vocabulary for pure mathematics history.

author_full_name: Peter P. Swire, Robert E. Litan
title: None of Your Business: World Data Flows, Electronic Commerce, and the European Privacy Directive
description:
None of Your Business is a legal and economic analysis of the European Union's 1995 Data Protection Directive. Swire and Litan wrote it as the Directive's October 1998 deadline approached and as the United States negotiated with Europe over the treatment of American companies' data practices.

The Directive bars transfer of Europeans' personal data to countries without "adequate" privacy protection, a standard the United States' sector-by-sector approach to privacy law did not obviously meet. The authors work through what an adverse adequacy finding would mean for the financial services industry and other sectors dependent on transborder data flows. The book lays out the Directive's legal text and background, the tension between the Directive and information technologies then emerging, and policy recommendations meant to avert a transatlantic trade dispute over privacy.

Swire, then a law professor at Ohio State University, had already written on cryptography and internet regulation and later served as a privacy official in the Clinton and Obama administrations. Litan directed the Economic Studies program at the Brookings Institution, which published the book in 1998.
tags: Privacy, Law

title: The War on the Bill of Rights and the Gathering Resistance
description:
The War on the Bill of Rights and the Gathering Resistance is Nat Hentoff's account of the expansion of government surveillance and detention power after September 11, 2001. He wrote it as the USA PATRIOT Act's provisions were being implemented and a second PATRIOT Act was under discussion in Washington.

Hentoff drew on interviews with reporters, defense attorneys, civil liberties lawyers, and administration officials. He documents surveillance programs including Carnivore and the Total Information Awareness system, the use of material-witness detention, and proposals that would have suspended habeas corpus or allowed revocation of citizenship. He pairs this with an account of the opposition the Act drew from an unusually broad range of critics, including conservative members of Congress. The book closes with suggestions for readers who want to push back against the measures it describes.

Hentoff wrote a syndicated column for decades and covered the First Amendment and the Bill of Rights for the Village Voice. At the time of this book, published by Seven Stories Press in 2003, he was also a senior fellow at the Cato Institute. It followed a long run of his writing on free speech and civil liberties, including Free Speech for Me But Not for Thee.
tags: Surveillance, Law, Privacy

title: Spying with Maps: Surveillance Technologies and the Future of Privacy
edition_printrun: First edition (a paperback edition followed, ISBN 9780226534282)
description:
Spying with Maps surveys the geographic surveillance technologies, satellite imagery, GPS tracking, and geographic information systems, that had by 2002 moved location monitoring from military and intelligence use into law enforcement, market research, and traffic engineering.

Monmonier explains how each technology works and who uses it before turning to the privacy questions it raises, a subject he treats as a genuinely new problem for cartography rather than as an occasion for alarm; reviewers described the book's approach to what he calls "dataveillance" as even-handed rather than as a warning of an Orwellian future. The University of Chicago Press published the hardcover in 2002 and later issued it in paperback.

Monmonier is a Distinguished Professor of Geography at Syracuse University's Maxwell School and the author of How to Lie with Maps and Bushmanders and Bullwinkles. Spying with Maps extends his long-running attention to the political uses and consequences of mapmaking into the era of satellite and location tracking.
tags: Surveillance, Privacy, GPS
notes: "GPS" added as a new tag; nothing in the existing fixed vocabulary covers geospatial/location tracking specifically.

title: Cryptography & Liberty 1999: An International Survey of Encryption Policy
description:
A country-by-country survey of encryption law and policy compiled by the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC) on behalf of the Global Internet Liberty Campaign (GILC), documenting the legal status of cryptography in seventy-six national and territorial jurisdictions as of 1999.

Most countries surveyed, industrial and developing alike, imposed no controls on the use, manufacture, or sale of cryptography. The report found a broad international trend toward relaxing what restrictions did exist. It also tracked a parallel rejection of key escrow and key recovery schemes, the approach then favored by the U.S. government. France had recently dropped its own escrow requirement, and other governments were declining to adopt one. Only a small number of countries, the report noted, kept strong domestic controls on cryptographic use. The survey updated an earlier 1998 report of the same title by Wayne Madsen, David L. Sobel, Marc Rotenberg, and David Banisar, published as a law-journal article. A further edition, Cryptography and Liberty 2000, followed it.

EPIC is a Washington, D.C. public-interest research organization focused on privacy and civil liberties in the information age, founded in 1994 by Marc Rotenberg and David Sobel. Through the late 1990s it was a leading participant in the U.S. cryptography-policy debate. It opposed the Clinton administration's Clipper Chip key-escrow initiative and export controls on strong encryption, and published this survey as part of its broader case against criminalizing encryption technology.
tags: Cryptography, Privacy, Law, Surveillance
notes: Authored/edited by EPIC staff Wayne Madsen and David Banisar (per the earlier 1998 journal-article version's byline and secondary sources on the 2000 follow-up), but published and credited on the title page as an EPIC organizational report; catalogued here under EPIC as the organizational author per the title page. No LOC or WorldCat record was located; bibliographic data is from AbeBooks (schema.org Book record) and OpenLibrary. Dimensions not found in any source consulted.

title: The First Amendment and the Fourth Estate: Communications Law for Undergraduates
description:
The second edition of a communications-law textbook Marc A. Franklin wrote for undergraduate journalism students, not law students. It surveys First Amendment doctrine and the legal problems reporters and broadcasters meet gathering and publishing news.

The book opens by reviewing the philosophical justifications for freedom of expression and the structure of the American judicial system. It then works through the legal problems journalists face gathering information and publishing what they gather. Its final chapters turn to broadcasting: the technology and regulatory structure of the industry, the licensing of broadcasters, and the content restrictions that apply to broadcast but not to print. The preface says the book organizes these problems the way working journalists and editors encounter them, not the way a law-school casebook would, and assumes no legal training. This second edition, published in 1981, revises Franklin's 1977 first edition, written with Ruth Korzenik Franklin. Robert Trager assisted on the revision.

Franklin was the Frederick I. Richman Professor of Law at Stanford University. He is best known for his long-running torts casebook with Robert Rabin. This undergraduate text grew into a separate law-school casebook, The First Amendment and the Fourth Estate: The Law of Mass Media. Franklin developed it with T. Barton Carter and Jay B. Wright, and it has run through more than a dozen editions since.
tags: Law
notes: No cover photograph could be confirmed. AbeBooks' schema.org record for this ISBN gives title/subtitle/author as "The First Amendment and the fourth estate: Communications law for undergraduates" / Franklin, Marc A. (matching this record). A separate AbeBooks dealer listing for the same ISBN instead credits Carter, T. Barton; Franklin, Marc A.; Wright, Jay B. That is almost certainly bookseller cross-contamination. A similarly titled, separately numbered companion casebook, "The First Amendment and the Fourth Estate: The Law of Mass Media" (Carter/Franklin/Wright), launched its own first edition the same year, 1981. OpenLibrary's MARC-derived edition record for this ISBN (by_statement "by Marc A. Franklin, assisted by Robert Trager", edition "2nd ed.", 715 pages) is used here as the more authoritative source. One dealer describes the binding as red cloth with gilt titling. That matches the 1977 first edition's binding, confirmed directly from a scanned copy, but no photograph of this specific 2nd-edition printing was located.

title: Secrets of a Super Hacker
description:
A how-to manual on breaking into computer systems, written under the pseudonym The Knightmare and published by the fringe press Loompanics Unlimited in 1994. It gives step-by-step instructions for social engineering, password theft, and system infiltration from a home computer, aimed at a reader with no prior hacking experience.

The book's core subject is social engineering: talking legitimate users and system administrators into giving up passwords and access. The author calls its variants reverse social engineering, spoofing, and superuser abuse. Further chapters cover screen stealing, hidden data delivery, Trojan horses, trap doors, and dummy accounts. Appendixes explain database and operating-system structure and password-guessing strategy, and close with a glossary of hacking terms. A closing chapter surveys the state and federal computer-crime laws a reader risked breaking by using the techniques described. Gareth Branwyn, an editor associated with the cyberpunk-era magazine Mondo 2000 and later a founding writer at Wired, supplies the introduction; Dan Wend illustrated it.

Loompanics Unlimited, the book's publisher, specialized in manuals on subjects mainstream houses avoided, from lock picking to fake identification. Secrets of a Super Hacker fits that catalog: an early, plainly written primer on hacking methodology rather than a technical security text. Some sources identify the author behind the Knightmare pseudonym as Dennis Fiery, itself understood to be another assumed name rather than the writer's legal identity.
tags: Hacking

title: Digital Evidence and Computer Crime: Forensic Science, Computers and the Internet
description:
The first edition of Eoghan Casey's foundational digital-forensics textbook, laying out how to locate, preserve, and interpret digital evidence. It covers how computer networks figure in crimes ranging from fraud and stalking to homicide and child exploitation.

Casey wrote the book to bridge four fields he saw as inseparable in practice: law, computer science, forensic science, and behavioral evidence analysis. Chapters cover the legal framework governing digital evidence, how computers and networks function well enough to locate and recover that evidence, and how to reconstruct events at a digital crime scene. Case examples, references to the specialized literature, and a glossary of terms run throughout. Susan W. Brenner and other contributors supplied material on the legal-issues chapters. Computer networks were becoming central to a widening range of offenses when the book appeared. It was among the first attempts to treat digital evidence with the same rigor as physical forensic evidence, rather than as a specialist add-on to traditional investigation.

Casey holds a Ph.D. in computer science from University College Dublin. He has moved between digital-forensics practice and research throughout his career: as information security officer at Yale University, lead cybersecurity engineer at MITRE, chief scientist at the Department of Defense Cyber Crime Center, and, later, professor of digital forensic science at the University of Lausanne. He has testified as an expert witness in criminal and civil cases and edited the journal Digital Investigation since 2004. This book's success led him to expand it substantially in later editions and to edit the companion Handbook of Computer Crime Investigation and Handbook of Digital Forensics and Investigation.
tags: Forensics, Law
notes: A second ISBN, 9780121631048, appears in dealer and OpenLibrary records for what is described as the same 1st-edition text (Academic Press, 279pp.) without the subtitle displayed; this may be a concurrent US/UK issue of the same edition rather than a distinct printing, but that could not be confirmed. Description above reflects the 1st edition (2000, 279pp.) specifically; later editions (2nd ed. 2004, 3rd ed. 2011/2017) were substantially expanded to roughly 800 pages with a five-part structure and additional contributors, and their content should not be conflated with this edition's.

title: The Spy's Guide: Office Espionage - How to Bug a Meeting, Booby-Trap Your Briefcase, Infiltrate the Competition, and More
description:
A tongue-in-cheek office-espionage manual that repackages real intelligence-agency tradecraft, from bugging a conference room to reassembling shredded documents, as workplace tactics for getting ahead. H. Keith Melton and television producer Craig Piligian wrote it with Duane Swierczynski, with a foreword by retired KGB Major General Oleg Kalugin.

Its premise, stated in the publisher's copy, is that information is the currency of business, and no one gathers it more effectively than spies. Illustrated, step-by-step sections cover planting bugs, tapping phones, disguising your identity at a trade show, sending untraceable e-mail, photographing confidential documents, encrypting an address book, and piecing together shredded paperwork. Each section pairs the technique with a real anecdote of the CIA, the KGB, or a Fortune 500 company using it. The tone throughout stays closer to a novelty gift book than a security manual, part of the same Quirk Books line as its companion, The Action Hero's Handbook.

Melton is a historian of espionage technology, the author of Ultimate Spy, and a board member of the International Spy Museum in Washington, D.C. The Hudson Street Library also holds his The Secret History of KGB Spy Cameras, 1945-1995, co-written with Vladimir Alekseenko. Piligian is an Emmy-winning television producer who has made several documentaries on espionage tradecraft. Swierczynski, credited as a contributing writer here, later became a bestselling and twice Edgar-nominated crime novelist.
tags: Espionage, Surveillance
notes: Page count is reported as 180 by one OpenLibrary edition and 165 by several bookseller listings; 165 is used here as the more consistently repeated figure, but this is not fully resolved.

title: The Well: A Story of Love, Death & Real Life in the Seminal Online Community
description:
A social history of the WELL (Whole Earth 'Lectronic Link), the San Francisco Bay Area dial-up bulletin board founded in 1985. It grew into one of the first sustained online communities, a proving ground for what people would later call internet culture.

Stewart Brand and Larry Brilliant founded the WELL and modeled it loosely on the salon. It drew journalists, programmers, Deadheads, and other early adopters into public conferences. Over years online, its members came to know each other with real intimacy. Hafner traces that history from the WELL's founding through its 1999 sale to Salon.com, expanding on a 1997 Wired cover story she wrote on the same subject. She builds the book around the on- and offline relationship between two WELL members she calls Mandel and Nana. That relationship runs through breakdown, illness, and death, and Hafner uses it to show how the boundary between a person's public online self and private life could dissolve inside the community. The book covers the WELL's triumphs and losses alike, including births, reunions, and the deaths of several members whose final illnesses played out in public on the system's message boards.

Hafner is a longtime technology reporter for The New York Times. She also wrote Where Wizards Stay Up Late: The Origins of the Internet, a history of ARPANET, and has covered cybercrime and hacking. The WELL was eclipsed in scale by the networks that followed it. Its close-knit, high-intimacy culture is still widely credited as a founding model for online community. Later writers, notably Howard Rheingold in The Virtual Community, cite it as a benchmark rarely matched by the larger, more anonymous forums that came after it.
tags: Internet Culture

title: GPS Made Easy: Using Global Positioning Systems in the Outdoors
description:
A non-technical guide to using handheld GPS receivers outdoors. It was revised after the U.S. government turned off Selective Availability in May 2000. That change alone improved unaided civilian accuracy from roughly 100 meters to under 10.

The book explains how the GPS satellite constellation and signal work. It surveys the features common to handheld receivers of the period. And it works through practical field examples: setting waypoints, plotting routes, and using a receiver alongside a paper topographic map in rough or featureless terrain. This third edition, marketed as "SA Revised," added material on the first two editions covering GPS with maps for hiking, kayaking, and other backcountry travel.

Lawrence Letham is an electrical engineer by training. He wrote the book for the hikers, campers, and outdoor navigators he counted himself among. GPS Made Easy went through five editions between the mid-1990s and 2008, tracking each new generation of consumer GPS technology from the pre-SA era through WAAS-corrected receivers.
tags: GPS, Reference
notes: AbeBooks' pictures.abebooks.com image for this ISBN (9780898868029) is mismatched: it actually shows the 5th-edition cover (co-authored with Alex Letham). The cover used here instead comes from OpenLibrary's cover API for this exact ISBN and correctly shows the third-edition, SA-revised cover.

title: The Essential Guide to Wireless Communications Applications: From Cellular Systems to Wi-Fi
description:
A nontechnical survey of consumer and business wireless technology, aimed at engineers, marketers, and investors. This second edition updates the book for 2002, past the WAP-and-m-commerce moment of the 2000 first edition.

Chapters cover wireless economics and industry structure, buying guidance for cellular phones and service plans, and setting up and securing wireless LANs. Others cover mobile commerce and payment systems, the leading handheld operating systems of the day (BlackBerry, Pocket PC, Palm, Tablet PC), and public concern over the health effects of wireless communications. The book arrived as 3G and 3.5G cellular networks, WLANs, and wireless optics were reaching a general business readership, not just engineers.

Andy Dornan was a senior editor covering wireless technology at Network Magazine in San Francisco. He has written on wireless and network security for Wired, Red Herring, and Dark Reading. This book followed his earlier Essential Guide to RF and Wireless.
tags: Wireless, Reference

title: Loose Lips
description:
A comic novel of CIA tradecraft training, published in 2003. It follows a young recruit through the agency's clandestine-service program at "the Farm."

Selena Keller is an unemployed New Yorker with a doctorate in Oriental studies and no clear career ahead of her. On a whim, she sends her resume to the CIA. An Agency recruiter asks her how she would feel about persuading another human being to commit treason. She passes the background investigation, the polygraph, and a battery of psychological aptitude tests, then begins an eighteen-month training program while living under cover as a government budget analyst. At the Farm she falls for a fellow trainee, Stan, a brilliant and increasingly paranoid classmate with presidential ambitions. The novel mixes satire, romance, and procedural detail on tradecraft and agency culture. On publication it was praised as an unusually candid, funny account of CIA training life, written from a woman's point of view.

Claire Berlinski is an American journalist and novelist educated at Balliol College, Oxford, where she took a doctorate in international relations. Loose Lips was her debut novel. She later published a second spy novel, Lion Eyes, alongside nonfiction political books including There Is No Alternative: Why Margaret Thatcher Matters and Menace in Europe.
tags: Fiction, Espionage
notes: Berlinski has not held a CIA position herself; the novel draws on research and reporting rather than personal agency employment. A later paperback (Ballantine Books, ISBN 9780812967098) reissued the same text as "Loose Lips: A Novel."

title: Alvin's Secret Code
description:
The second Alvin Fernald novel, published in 1963 with line illustrations by Bill Sokol. Twelve-year-old Alvin and his friend Shoie turn a self-taught grounding in codes and ciphers into a full treasure hunt.

The two boys, calling themselves secret agents, intercept a coded message and cannot break it themselves. They seek out Mr. Link, a retired code expert, who teaches them cipher wheels, the scytale, and other classical methods. The arrival of a woman in distress and a mysterious stranger draws Alvin, Shoie, and Alvin's younger sister into a hundred-year-old town mystery and a scheme against a local orphanage. It ends in a hunt for buried treasure, which Alvin's "Magnificent Brain" resolves through his own improvised cipher. An appendix at the back lays out the codes, ciphers, and code wheel used in the story for readers to try themselves.

Clifford B. Hicks was a Popular Mechanics editor and a Silver Star-decorated Marine veteran of World War II. He introduced Alvin Fernald in 1960 with The Marvelous Inventions of Alvin Fernald. Alvin's Secret Code was the second of what grew into a long-running series, later adapted into two Disney television movies.

title: The First Book of Codes and Ciphers
description:
An introductory primer on codes and ciphers for young readers, published in 1956 as part of Franklin Watts's "First Book" series, with drawings by Laszlo Roth. It opens by distinguishing the two methods of secret writing it covers throughout: a code, which substitutes symbols for whole words or phrases, and a cipher, which substitutes symbols for individual letters.

Short chapters move from a reader's first attempt at a simple substitution code through the Caesar cipher, a backward cipher, and a cipher the authors identify in the Bible. Later chapters cover number ciphers, the semaphore and Morse codes, the ogam script of the Celts, and the breaking of a Spanish king's cipher. Others take up the Rosetta Stone, invisible inks, business codes, and codes used in detective fiction. The book closes with an answer key and index. Contemporary listings describe it as issued in gray buckram boards with the title lettered on the spine and front board.

Sam and Beryl Epstein were a husband-and-wife writing team. From 1938 onward they published more than 120 children's nonfiction titles and biographies together, including many entries in Franklin Watts's First Book series. Under several joint pseudonyms they also wrote the Ken Holt mystery series.

title: The Clue in the Crossword Cipher
description:
Book forty-four in the Nancy Drew Mystery Stories series, first published in 1967. It sends Nancy to Peru to decode a cipher carved into an ancient wooden plaque, before a smuggling ring can reach the treasure it points to.

Carla Ponce, a young woman living in Peru, invites Nancy, Bess, and George to help solve her family's "monkey mystery." It centers on a wooden plaque bearing a crossword cipher that time has largely worn away. A gang led by a smuggler known as El Gato steals the plaque, so Nancy has to recover it before she can even begin decoding it. Her investigation carries her to the Incan ruins at Cuzco and Machu Picchu. There she and her friends help break up the smuggling ring and turn up an archaeological find of their own.

Carolyn Keene is the house pseudonym the Stratemeyer Syndicate, and later Grosset & Dunlap and Simon & Schuster, used across the entire Nancy Drew series. Individual volumes were written by a rotating set of ghostwriters under contract, beginning with Mildred Wirt Benson on the earliest titles. This catalogue follows its own convention for house pseudonyms and credits the byline as printed, not an individual ghostwriter.
